newsitem.title: USA: Dole advisers critical of Clinton Iraq policy.
newsitem.headline: Dole advisers critical of Clinton Iraq policy.

text.p: A top foreign policy adviser to Republican candidate Bob Dole accused President Bill Clinton on Thursday of giving Iraq "a free pass" by allowing its troops to remain in the Kurdish safe zone in northern Iraq.

Paul Wolfowitz, an assistant secretary of state and deputy secretary of defence under Republican presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush, also said Clinton failed to generate broad allied support for the missile strikes because they were "little pinprick attacks" that would not get the job done.

Wolfowitz and former U.N. Ambassador Jeanne Kirkpatrick, another Dole adviser, criticised Clinton's foreign policy during a luncheon of the Overseas Writers organisation here, expressing views that Republican presidential nominee Dole would have a stronger foreign policy than Clinton.

Clinton said on Wednesday two rounds of missile strikes at Iraqi military sites that were ordered after Iraqi troops moved into the Kurdish zone achieved the U.S. mission even though Iraqi troops remained in the north.
Secretary of State Warren Christopher also said the United States did not expect Saddam to withdraw all his troops from the north.

Wolfowitz, now dean of Johns Hopkins University Nitze School of Advanced International Studies, said he was speaking for himself and not Dole -- and accused the Clinton administration of abandoning the north to Saddam.

"I think they (the administration) are trying to declare victory ... and in the course of justifying this victory they are saying something which does enormous further damage, which is saying the north doesn't matter," he said.
"For five years we've been getting people to put their lives on the line on the grounds it matters to keep Saddam out of the north," he said. "... and now we're told it doesn't matter."
He said "it is very very damaging to American credibility now to give them a free pass on Iraqi troops when our objective ought to get them out."
Wolfowitz said "It will be difficult but it will be impossible (to force troops out) when the secretary of state essentially writes it off."
He added, "We did it in 1991 ... We moved the whole Iraqi army out of the north in 1991 without a single shot being fired. It may be more difficult now but it is impossible when you write it off."
On the limited allied support for the raids, Wolfowitz took the position that Clinton failed to persuade allies that the proposed U.S. action would get the job done.
"We cannot persuade people whose vital interests are at risk to go along with little pinprick attacks of the kind we've just seen in the last few days," he said.
Wolfowitz said Bush convinced allies like Saudi Arabia to back the Gulf War because he "persuaded them in his words that he would finish the job."
